1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4.name: Sicilian Defence: Open
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes White's d-pawn from the centre in return for Black's c-pawn: Black trades a wing pawn for a central one. After White recaptures, Black has two centre pawns against one, and the fight is about who profits from that.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 e6.name: Sicilian Defence: Franco-Sicilian Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 e6.strategy: Aims at control of d5, but cannot stop White from advancing there at once: the pawn attacks the knight and drives it away, gaining space with tempo. Black's pieces end up pushed back.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 d6.strategy: Guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop, but does not answer the tension in the centre: 4.d5 drives the knight back to b8 and gains space. Black has lost two moves with the same piece, and White has the freer game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.name: Sicilian Defence: Open
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which stands in the centre with open lines for all of White's pieces. White has fewer central pawns but more activity; the knights on d4 and c6 face each other, and neither side wants to trade first.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.strategy: A pawn gambit: White offers the c-pawn for open lines and quick development, and recaptures with a piece if Black takes. It is playable but second-rate here, since White pays a pawn for a lead in development that Black can answer with careful play.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Loses the queen: the knight on c6 attacks d4, so ...Nxd4 wins it, and the recapture on d4 returns only a knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Open
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.strategy: The main line. The knight develops with a threat to the unprotected e4 pawn, so White has to deal with it, usually by developing the knight to c3, which also takes the c4 square away from White. Black keeps the pawn structure flexible.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6.name: Sicilian Defence: Accelerated Dragon
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6.background: Kennedy against Wyvill in 1851 is an early game with it. It became popular in the twentieth century as a way to reach a Dragon set-up while avoiding the Yugoslav Attack, its ultimate test, at the price of allowing the Maróczy Bind.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, ...Nf6 and castling without spending a move on ...d6, so ...d5 stays available in one move. Black avoids the most dangerous direct attack, but accepts that White can clamp the centre with c4 and play a cramped, manoeuvring game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5.name: Sicilian Defence: Löwenthal Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5.background: It was first played by La Bourdonnais in his matches against McDonnell in 1834.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5.strategy: Kicks the knight away at once and claims the centre. In return Black accepts a weak square on d5 and a backward d-pawn, while White's knight gets a forward post from which to attack the d6 square.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Qc7.name: Sicilian Defence: Flohr Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Qc7.strategy: Puts the queen on the c-file, where it supports the knight and prepares to meet the centre with ...e6 without committing the d-pawn. Solid and flexible, but it gives up the more active knight development and lets White build the centre as it wishes.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Qb6.name: Sicilian Defence: Godiva Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Qb6.strategy: Attacks the knight a second time (the knight on c6 already hits it) and eyes the b2 pawn, so the natural defence with the bishop drops that pawn. White simply retreats the knight, and the queen has come out early without achieving much.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6.strategy: Takes b5 away from White's knight and prepares queenside play, but does nothing for development and lets White clamp the centre. A slow, useful move rather than a challenge to the position.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 d5.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzo-American Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre before the pieces are out. White can steer into a queenless position, or take on d5 and chase the queen with developing moves, so Black's early break costs more than it gains.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5..strategy: Clamps down on d5 with pawns on c4 and e4. With Black's ...a6 already played, the bind is easy to establish: White gets a space advantage and makes Black's freeing ...d5 break hard to achieve, at the price of a weakened d4 square.

Develops the second knight and defends e4 without committing a pawn. White keeps the knight's central post on d4 and decides about the bishop later, so the game stays flexible and Black has to show which set-up it wants.

A modest developing move that prepares castling but asks Black no question. It leaves Black free to finish development at ease and does nothing for the centre, so White gives up the chance to set the agenda.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Maróczy Bind, Geller Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5..strategy: Challenges the knight and takes space in the centre. With White's pawns on c4 and e4 holding the d5 square, Black accepts a backward d-pawn and a hole that White's bind keeps under control.

Develops with a threat: the knight attacks the e4 pawn, which nothing protects, so White must defend it before anything else. Black keeps the breaks ...b5 and ...d5 in mind and can ease the cramp of the pawns on c4 and e4 by trading knights.
Controls d5 and opens the f8-bishop, so Black can meet the clamp of c4 and e4 with piece play. The price is a slightly passive centre that does not hit e4, so White finishes development in peace.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5..strategy: The critical reply: the knight leaves the centre and aims at the weakened d6 square, where it would land with check and cost Black the bishop pair. White gains time and the initiative.
Retreats the knight, its third move, away from the attack of the e5 pawn without gaining anything. Black keeps the central pawns and White a solid but passive position.

Trades the knight, which the e5 pawn attacks, for Black's. Black recaptures with a pawn and keeps a broad pawn centre and a half-open b-file, so White gets no lead and no target: a safe but toothless way out of the attack.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Kalashnikov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5..background: In the late 1980s Black players revived 4...e5 with the intention of meeting 5.Nb5 with 5...d6; it was popularised by Evgeny Sveshnikov and is now significantly more popular than the older 5...a6.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5..strategy: Closes the d6 square at once and accepts the structural trade: a backward d-pawn and a hole on d5 for the time gained chasing the stray knight on b5. Neither side has committed its knights yet, which leaves both with more choices.

Develops with a threat on e4, so White cannot simply jump to d6: after the exchange there, the knight takes e4 with an attack on the queen. White first has to defend the pawn, and Black develops with a gain of time.
Attacks the knight at once, but if it jumps to d6 Black gives up the bishop pair, and White kept an edge in several lines. A playable but second-rate try next to the more popular ...d6.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Accelerated Dragon, Maróczy Bind
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..background: The first game known to feature the Maróczy Bind is Swiderski against Maróczy, Monte Carlo 1904. For several decades it was generally considered tantamount to a blunder for Black to allow it; from the 1950s new methods made it less feared.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..strategy: The most testing line: pawns on c4 and e4 clamp down on the d5 square, making Black's freeing ...d5 break difficult and giving White a space advantage. The game becomes a slow manoeuvring battle in which Black has to find counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and defends e4, keeping the position sharp. Black can reach the ...d5 break a tempo sooner because ...d6 has not been spent, so a direct attack is less dangerous for Black here, and White gives up the idea of the bind.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Accelerated Dragon, Exchange Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..strategy: Trades off the knight that guards d4 and e5, but after ...bxc6 the pawn on c6 supports ...d5 and the bishop is free to develop. The queen sortie that hits the h8 rook looks flashy and leaves Black comfortable.

Develops the bishop to a post that defends the knight on d4 and keeps White's options open. It is flexible, but it claims no space as c4 does, so Black can complete the fianchetto in peace and prepare the freeing ...d5 break.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop now attacks the knight on d4 together with the knight on c6, adding to the pressure on the centre. The king can castle once the knight is out, and Black stays flexible about the pawn structure.
Develops with a threat on e4, which nothing protects, so White must defend the pawn at once. Black keeps the quick ...d5 break in reserve, since the d-pawn has not moved.
The solid pawn move that gives up the quick ...d5 break: it guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop but commits Black to a slower set-up, in which White can choose between a quiet game and a sharp attack.
Prepares to castle, but is slow: Black develops, castles and strikes in the centre with ...d5, which equalises without difficulty.

Develops the knight and defends e4, the traditional set-up of the opening, in which White then develops the bishop actively and castles. The play is sharp and tactical and White has to be accurate: Black's ...d5 break is in hand whenever White is slow.

Clamps down on d5 with pawns on c4 and e4, making Black's freeing ...d5 break hard to achieve and gaining space. The price is a permanently weak square on d4; Black plays for exchanges and counterplay against the cramp.
Develops with an attack on e4 and prepares to castle, after which the freeing ...d5 break is only one move away. A natural, harmonious set-up.
Guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop in a compact set-up, but gives up the quick ...d5 break that a delayed d-pawn is meant to keep. Black takes the quieter road and White is not troubled in the centre.

Simplifies at once by trading a pair of knights. White recaptures with the bishop, which lands on d4 facing the g7-bishop; Black must allow it to sit there or trade the dark-squared bishops, the piece the whole set-up depends on.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Accelerated Dragon, Maróczy Bind
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..strategy: The main line: completes the fianchetto and puts the bishop on the diagonal towards d4 before White has chosen where to put the pieces. Black accepts the cramp of the bind and plans to relieve it with exchanges and counterplay.

Develops with an attack on e4, so White has to reinforce it by developing the knight. Black aims to trade knights on d4 to relieve the cramp of the bind, and because White's bishop is not yet on e3, the queen has to recapture.
A solid pawn move that guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop, but it gives up the quick ...d5 break that the accelerated move order saved. Black accepts the bind with a compact but passive set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Accelerated Dragon, Maróczy Bind
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5..strategy: The main line: the bishop defends the knight on d4 and develops, so White meets a knight trade with a recapture by a minor piece rather than by the queen. White keeps the bind and plays for a lasting space advantage.
Retreats the knight to avoid the exchanges that would relieve Black's cramp, keeping the bind intact. It looks passive, but it keeps more pieces on the board and aims to keep Black short of space.

Steps back to a safe square before the knight can be traded, so Black's cramp stays and all the minor pieces remain on the board. From b3 the knight covers a5 and c5, but it is less active than on d4 and costs time, which lets Black organise the usual counterplay on the wings.
Develops with an attack on e4 and prepares castling. Black's counterplay comes from exchanges that ease the cramp and from pawn breaks on the wings, since the central ...d5 is hard to achieve.

Solidifies the centre and opens the c8 bishop, keeping the knight move for later. It is sound, but it commits the d-pawn before Black knows where the pieces belong and leaves White a free choice of set-up.

Trades the knight that cramps Black at once. The bishop recaptures with a hit on g7, and if the dark-squared bishops then come off, White's queen lands on d4 with a threat against the h8 rook. Black eases the cramp, but White gains time for development.
Solidifies the centre and gives the bishop on c8 a diagonal. With the knight retreated, Black can look for space and counterplay through pawn breaks on the wings, with a solid game.
Develops with a hit on e4 and prepares to castle, so White must spend a move guarding the pawn. Black gets a natural, flexible position and can decide the pawn structure later.

Gains space on the queenside and takes b4 away from White's pawns, which stops White expanding there with the b-pawn. The move develops nothing and leaves b6 without a pawn guard, so it suits Black as part of a slower plan.

Defends e4 against the knight on f6 and adds a third guard of d5, which completes the clamp on Black's centre. Black's freeing ...d5 push is all but ruled out, so Black must look for counterplay elsewhere, in a slow manoeuvring game in which White keeps the extra space.

Trades the d4 knight at once, before Black can choose the moment. After ...bxc6 Black has a pawn that fights for d5 and a half-open b-file, which eases the cramp the bind is meant to cause, while the e4 pawn still needs a defender.
Retreats the knight to avoid exchanges but leaves e4 unguarded: ...Nxe4 wins a clean pawn, and the knight can step back to safety if it is attacked.

Trades off White's best-placed piece at once to ease the cramp. With no bishop on e3 yet, only the queen can recapture, and it is drawn to d4, where Black can try to gain time against it. White keeps the space, but Black develops freely.

The main way to meet the bind: it opens the c8 bishop and keeps the knight trade in reserve. When the knights come off, White's queen has to recapture, and Black can harass it as the pieces come out. Black accepts a cramped but sturdy position and plays against the queenside pawns.

Develops the bishop at once, hoping to reach the main bind position by transposition. But the knight on f6 blocks the bishop's diagonal, and White can trade on c6 and drive the knight away with the e-pawn, gaining time and space.

The essential move of the set-up: the fianchettoed bishop eyes the d4 knight and the long diagonal, and Black prepares to castle. Because the d-pawn has not moved, ...d5 can still be played in a single move, which makes White's attacking plans less dangerous than against the usual Dragon.

Heads for the ordinary Dragon set-up with the knight already on c6, where White's sharpest attacking plan with long castling is available. Sound, but it spends a pawn move the opening was designed to avoid and gives up the one-move ...d5.
Hits e4 at once, but White trades on c6 and drives the knight back with the e-pawn, winning time and space. The bishop on g7 is the move this set-up needs first.

Supports the d4 knight, which the bishop on g7 attacks, and prepares to castle long. The aggressive set-up with pawn storm on the kingside is less effective here, since Black can answer it with ...d5 in a single move; White usually needs a more careful way to place the pieces.

Steps back before the knight can be traded, keeping all the minor pieces and covering a5 and c5. White gives up the active post for a modest set-up, and Black develops without trouble, with the bishop on g7 already bearing on the c3 knight.
A quiet retreat that keeps the c3 knight and offers no trade on d4. The knight blocks the f1 bishop for now and White gives up the initiative, so Black can develop freely and play for equality.

Brings the last kingside piece out with pressure on e4 and gets ready to castle. Black keeps the d-pawn at home so that ...d5 stays a one-move strike, and White has to place the bishop and castle with care or be hit in the centre.

Plays the pawn at once, steering into an ordinary Dragon set-up with the knight already on c6. It solidifies the centre and frees the c8 bishop, but it gives up the one-move ...d5 that makes this move order attractive and lets White choose the attacking set-up.
Trades knights, but 7.Bxd4 attacks the undefended bishop on g7, and after 7...Bxd4 8.Qxd4 the rook on h8 is attacked as well. Black is left defending the long diagonal and stands clearly worse.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Defends the e4 pawn that the knight attacks and develops the second knight, keeping the strong knight on d4. White hands Black the central question: a solid pawn structure, or a lunge that kicks the d4 knight at once.

Trades the d4 knight at once, giving Black a pawn recapture and a half-open b-file. The e4 pawn is attacked by the knight on f6 and needs a defender, after which Black takes the centre with a pawn and equalises without difficulty.
Guards e4 but blocks the queen's view of d4: Black simply takes the knight with ...Nxd4, and White cannot recapture.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Lasker-Pelikan Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.background: Also called the Sveshnikov Variation, after Evgeny Sveshnikov, who pioneered it with Gennadi Timoshchenko in the 1970s. Before that it saw only occasional play: Emanuel Lasker played it once in his world championship match against Carl Schlechter, and Jorge Pelikan a few times in the 1950s. Today it is extremely popular among grandmasters and amateurs alike.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Kicks the d4 knight and stakes a claim in the centre at once. The price is a backward d-pawn and a lasting hole on d5, which White's pieces can occupy; in return Black gets active pieces and dynamic play, and White's knight is often driven to the edge of the board.

Supports the centre with the d-pawn, controls e5 and keeps Black's structure flexible. Black gives up the immediate kick at the d4 knight, and with it the active play, for a sound pawn set-up in which White chooses the plan, a quiet build-up or a sharp attack.

Opens the diagonal for the f8 bishop and covers d5 and f5, giving a sound pawn structure with no weakness. Black gives up the dynamic lunge at the knight and the activity that comes with it, and must watch the d6 square, which a white knight on b5 and the queen can both target.

The critical reply: the knight leaves with the threat of Nd6+, after which ...Bxd6 Qxd6 leaves a white queen cramping Black's whole position. White's long-term trump is the d5 hole; the price is a knight away from the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Lasker-Pelikan Variation, Retreat Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Retreats the knight and concedes that the kick on e5 was a gain of time. The f8 bishop is free to go to b4, where it pins the c3 knight and makes e4 a real target. White gets nothing for the lost time and Black equalises comfortably.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Lasker-Pelikan Variation, Schlechter Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Retreats the knight to the queenside, where it stops ...Bc5 but does little else. Black plays ...Bb4 instead, pinning the c3 knight and putting the e4 pawn under real pressure, and the knight on b3 does not help to defend it. Easy equality for Black.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Lasker-Pelikan Variation, Exchange Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Trades the strong knight at once. After ...bxc6 Black has a central pawn that covers d5, the square White was aiming at, so White gets no edge. Sound, but it gives up the pressure that makes Ndb5 the critical reply.

Shuts the d6 square against Nd6+, at the price of the concession that comes with ...e5: a backward d-pawn and a permanent hole on d5. The knight on b5 is out on a limb, and Black plays for activity and time rather than a perfect structure.

Pins the c3 knight to the king, but White checks on d6 at once. Black does best to take with the bishop, so the pin is gone, and the queen recaptures on d6 to cramp Black's position while White keeps both bishops.
Ignores the threat on d6. After 7.Nd6+ Bxd6 8.Qxd6 White has both bishops against one, and a queen on d6 that stops Black castling and cramps the whole position. The pawn move is a lost tempo.
